subject: English
stem: The central argument of the passage is that:
options: Routine, framework-preserving work is essential to progress, yet the very consensus that enables it can blind a science to contrary evidence until anomalies force a crisis.
Scientists are fundamentally dishonest about their data.
Scientific revolutions happen suddenly and without warning.
A mature science should abandon its framework whenever a single observation fails to fit.
passage: For most of its working life, a mature science behaves less like a restless explorer than like a careful accountant. Its practitioners are not, on the whole, trying to overturn the framework they inherited; they are trying to extend it, to tidy its edges, to force reluctant observations into the boxes the theory has already prepared. This unglamorous labour is not a failing but the very condition of progress: only a community that agrees on what counts as a legitimate problem, and on what would count as a solution, can accumulate the fine-grained results on which any deeper understanding must rest. Yet the same agreement that makes such precision possible also breeds a peculiar blindness. Observations that refuse to fit are, for a long time, not so much rejected as unseen — set aside as errors of measurement, as noise, as problems for someone else on some later day. An anomaly becomes a crisis only when it can no longer be quarantined, when it multiplies and begins to touch the framework's load-bearing assumptions. It is at that point, and rarely before, that a discipline becomes willing to entertain the once-unthinkable thought that the trouble lies not in the stubborn facts but in the theory itself. The revolutions we later celebrate as sudden were, almost always, preceded by years in which the decisive evidence sat in plain view and was simply not counted.

stem: The passage uses the pasture chiefly as:
options: An illustration of how individually rational choices can produce a collectively ruinous outcome when costs are shared but gains are private.
A nostalgic image of a vanished rural way of life.
A literal argument about the best way to raise cattle.
Evidence that herdsmen are unusually greedy people.
passage: Imagine a pasture open to all. Each herdsman, reasoning as any sensible person would, notices that adding one more animal to his own herd brings him the full value of that animal, while the cost of the extra grazing — the slow exhaustion of the common field — is shared among everyone. The private gain is concentrated and immediate; the public cost is diffuse and deferred. And so each herdsman, acting with impeccable individual rationality, adds another beast, and another, until the pasture that could have fed them all indefinitely is grazed to ruin. The tragedy, in the older and sterner sense of that word, is that it unfolds not through malice or stupidity but through the faithful pursuit of self-interest by people who can each see the ending and are each powerless, alone, to prevent it. What makes the problem so resistant to easy solution is that appeals to conscience are not merely ineffective but perverse: the herdsman who restrains himself for the common good simply cedes the grass to his less scrupulous neighbours, so that self-denial is punished and greed rewarded. This is why the more durable remedies have tended to involve not exhortation but structure — enforceable limits, assigned rights, mutual coercion mutually agreed upon — arrangements that change the arithmetic each individual faces rather than merely lecturing him about the sum.

stem: The central claim of the passage is that:
options: Information has become too expensive for ordinary people to obtain.
Entertainment is the main purpose of the modern information industry.
People today simply lack the willpower their ancestors had.

passage: There is a peculiar economics governing the modern world, and its scarce resource is neither money nor land but attention. When information was hard to come by, the person who possessed it held the advantage; today, when information is effectively infinite and free, the advantage passes to whoever can capture the fixed and stubbornly limited hours of human notice. This inversion has consequences we are only beginning to understand. An industry has grown up whose entire business is not to inform us, nor to entertain us for its own sake, but to hold our gaze long enough to sell it on to someone else. The most sophisticated minds of a generation, it has been remarked, now spend their days engineering the small compulsions that keep a thumb scrolling. We are inclined to blame ourselves for the hours that vanish this way, to treat our distraction as a private failure of willpower. But this is to misread the contest badly. It is not a fair fight between an individual's self-control and a passing temptation; it is a fight between one tired person and thousands of talented engineers equipped with the most detailed map of human impulse ever assembled. To call the outcome a failure of willpower is rather like calling a flooded village a failure of swimming.

stem: The main argument of the passage is that:
options: The capacity to be bored — to leave the mind unoccupied — has hidden value for creativity that the constant filling of every idle moment destroys.
Screens are the only reliable cure for boredom.

passage: We have been taught to regard boredom as a void to be filled at the first opportunity, an itch that the nearest screen exists to scratch. The restless, unoccupied mind is not merely idling; left alone, it begins to wander, to make unexpected connections, to worry at half-formed problems that a busier mind would never have the leisure to notice. Many who have thought carefully about creative work report that their best ideas arrived not at the desk but in its absence — on a walk, in the bath, in the drowsy minutes before sleep — precisely when the mind was permitted to roam without a task. Boredom, on this view, is not the enemy of a rich inner life but one of its unlikeliest tutors — and a civilisation that has abolished it may find it has thrown out something it did not know it possessed.

stem: The central argument of the passage is that:
options: Confidence and competence are the same thing.
Doubt, far from being a weakness, is the disposition that actually drives the growth of knowledge.
Certainty is always a sign of a well-educated mind.
One should doubt absolutely everything and act on nothing.
passage: We are trained, almost from infancy, to admire certainty and to be uneasy in the presence of the person who says, plainly, 'I do not know.' Confidence is mistaken for competence, and hesitation for weakness. Yet the history of thought suggests very nearly the opposite. The dogmatist, secure in his conclusions, has no reason to inquire further; having arrived, he stops. It is the doubter — the one willing to hold even his firmest convictions loosely — who keeps looking, and so keeps finding. Doubt, properly understood, is not the enemy of knowledge but its most faithful servant. It is the small, nagging suspicion that the accepted answer might be incomplete which has driven every genuine advance, from the overturning of ancient astronomy to the humblest correction of a household error. This is not to recommend a paralysing scepticism that doubts everything and therefore does nothing; that is merely dogmatism turned inside out. What is wanted is the harder discipline of proportioned belief — holding each conviction exactly as firmly as the evidence warrants, and no more. The truly educated mind is not the one crammed with the greatest number of certainties, but the one that has learned, in the face of a difficult question, to bear the discomfort of not yet knowing.

passage: A curious feature of ideas is that they disobey the ordinary laws of property. If I give you my umbrella, I no longer have it; but if I give you my idea, we both possess it entire, and between us it may breed a dozen more. This simple asymmetry explains much about why human progress has clustered so stubbornly in cities. A city is, above all, a device for multiplying the chance encounters out of which new ideas are struck — the overheard remark, the argument in a coffee-house, the rival glimpsed at work and quietly bettered. Density does for thought what a crowded market does for trade. The lone genius, toiling in isolation, is a romantic fiction; in practice, the isolated thinker is starved of exactly the friction and correction that a crowd of peers supplies. It is no accident that the great flowerings of art and science — classical Athens, Renaissance Florence, the coffee-house culture of the Enlightenment — occurred in places where clever people were packed close enough to irritate and inspire one another in roughly equal measure. Where minds are crowded together, the collisions are more frequent, and it is from such collisions, far more than from solitary reflection, that the genuinely new tends to emerge.

passage: Water has always been treated as the one resource nature would never let us run short of. For centuries, rivers were diverted, wells were dug, and rains were awaited with quiet confidence that the cycle would repeat itself, generation after generation, without much effort on our part. That confidence is no longer warranted. Groundwater tables in large parts of the country have fallen by tens of metres within a single lifetime, and cities that once boasted of lakes and stepwells now import water by tanker in the summer months. The crisis is not one of absolute scarcity so much as of mismanagement: rainfall over a year, if captured and stored efficiently, would be more than adequate for most regions. What is missing is not water but the discipline to conserve it, the infrastructure to store it, and the will to price it so that it is neither wasted by the profligate nor denied to the poor. Traditional systems of water harvesting, dismissed as primitive by planners in the decades after independence, are being rediscovered today precisely because they solved, cheaply and locally, a problem that centralised piped supply has struggled to solve at scale. The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a civilisation enamoured of technological solutions: sometimes the answer lies not in inventing something new but in re-learning what was once common knowledge and needlessly abandoned.

subject: English
stem: The passage argues that effective military leadership is primarily built on:
options: Shared risk, competence under fire, and genuine concern for one's men, which together earn trust.
Strict enforcement of rank and hierarchy.
The ability to issue orders without being questioned.
Harsh discipline that leaves no room for dissent.
passage: Leadership in uniform is often imagined as a matter of command: the ability to give an order and have it obeyed without question. This is a shallow reading of what makes an officer effective, particularly in conditions of extreme stress. Soldiers who have served under genuinely capable leaders describe something quite different from mere authority — they speak of an officer who ate what they ate, marched when they marched, and was seen forward of the position he was defending rather than behind it. Trust of this kind cannot be manufactured by rank alone; it is earned through a visible sharing of risk and hardship. Historians of warfare have long noted that units with the highest morale are rarely those with the harshest discipline, but those whose commanders demonstrated competence under fire and genuine concern for the welfare of their men. This does not mean that discipline is unimportant — an army without it dissolves into a mob — but that discipline sustained by fear is brittle, while discipline sustained by respect endures the worst that a battlefield can offer. The finest military traditions, across very different armies and eras, converge on this single insight: command is granted by rank, but leadership must be earned afresh, every single day, in the eyes of those who are asked to follow.

stem: What does the passage suggest about how soldiers typically remember the outcome of a battle?
options: As an inevitable result decided long before the fighting began.
As something they rarely think about afterwards.
As a matter decided by a series of small, uncertain moments rather than any predetermined outcome.
As entirely determined by which side had more soldiers.
passage: It is easy, looking back at a war from the safety of decades, to imagine that victory was inevitable and defeat foreordained. Soldiers who actually fought rarely describe it that way. What they remember, more often, is a string of moments in which the outcome hung on something as small as a signal received a few minutes late, a bridge held one hour longer than planned, or a reserve company committed at exactly the right time instead of five minutes too soon. Military historians have a name for this: the fog of war, the simple fact that no commander, however brilliant, ever has complete information about what is happening even a few kilometres away. passage: Games and sports have an important place in the life of a student. Many people think that the only duty of a student is to study his books and pass his examinations. This is a mistake. A student who spends all his time bent over his books, and never steps out into the playground, may do well in his examinations, but he often grows weak in body and dull in mind. Games keep the body fit and the mind fresh. A short game in the evening drives away the tiredness of a long day's study and sends the student back to his books with new energy. But the benefits of games are not limited to health alone. On the playing field a student learns lessons that no classroom can teach him. He learns to obey the captain, to play fair, to keep his temper when he loses, and to work with others for the good of his team. These are the very qualities that he will need in later life, when the playground of childhood has given way to the harder field of the world. A good player, it is often said, makes a good citizen.

stem: Why does the author call a good book 'a faithful friend'?
options: Because books can quarrel with us.

passage: The habit of reading is one of the greatest pleasures that a person can enjoy, and also one of the most useful. A good book is a faithful friend. It never grows tired of us, never quarrels with us, and is always ready to keep us company when we are lonely. Through books we can travel to distant lands without leaving our chairs, and meet the wisest men and women of every age, though they died hundreds of years ago. A person who has learned to love reading is never quite alone and never quite without resources. He can turn to a book for knowledge when he is puzzled, for comfort when he is sad, and for entertainment when he is bored. But like every good habit, the love of reading must be formed early and formed with care. Those who read nothing but cheap and worthless books gain little from the hours they spend, for the mind takes the shape of what it feeds upon. To choose one's books wisely is, therefore, almost as important as to read them at all.

passage: We speak of memory as if it were a recording, faithfully stored and replayed on demand. The evidence points the other way. Each act of recollection is less a retrieval than a reconstruction, assembled afresh from fragments and, in the assembling, quietly altered. What we take to be a vivid memory of an event is often a memory of the last time we recalled it, with each retelling laying down a fresh version that overwrites the old. The confidence we feel bears no reliable relation to accuracy; the most vivid and certain memories are as prone to distortion as the hazy ones, and sometimes more so, for their very vividness discourages doubt. This is not a defect to be lamented so much as the price of a system built for use rather than for the archive. A memory that updated itself with every fresh experience served our ancestors better than a perfect but rigid record would have. subject: English
stem: The two drivers are described primarily in order to:
options: expose a clash between how we claim to judge and how we really do
show that careless drivers are usually punished far too leniently by the courts
argue that luck plays no real part at all in questions of moral blame
prove that using a phone while driving should carry a much heavier penalty
passage: Consider two drivers, equally careless, who each glance down at a phone for the same reckless instant. On the first driver's road a child happens to step out, and is killed; on the second's, the road happens to be empty, and nothing occurs. The law will treat these two very differently, and so, if we are honest, will we: the first we are inclined to call a killer, the second merely a fool who got away with it. Yet the only difference between them lies in something wholly outside their control — the presence or absence of a child neither could have foreseen. This is the puzzle philosophers have called moral luck. We like to believe that a person can be judged only for what lies within his will, and that the workings of chance should make no difference to praise or blame. Our actual practice flatly contradicts this comforting principle at every turn. We heap censure on the reckless driver who is unlucky and quietly forgive the one who is not, though their choices were identical. To resolve the tension we must give up one of two convictions we are each loath to surrender: either that we are answerable only for what we control, or that outcomes rightly bear on how harshly we are judged. The discomfort of the problem lies precisely in our reluctance to abandon either.

passage: When Elizabeth Long began investigating women's book groups in the mid-1980s, her research plan provoked two profoundly different sets of reactions. Women, who had themselves participated in such groups, as well as men whose mothers and grandmothers had done so, immediately grasped the importance of her project: “You will never know what a difference it made” was the phrase she heard again and again. But among her academic colleagues, common readers seemed to be occupying a zone of cultural invisibility. They were not of interest to literature departments, whose major focus is on books and authors, not readers. They were not of interest to sociologists or political scientists because women's reading groups do not pursue activities with any obvious relationship to formal political processes. Long, however, went on to show that such groups had mobilised the women's suffrage and Progressive movements at the grassroots. Scholars of popular culture had not found reading groups interesting because the groups read canonized fiction and did not transform their cultural consumption into a 'resistant' subcultural style. It had not yet occurred to them that the so-called highbrow canonical literature could be immensely popular and devilishly subversive. David Vincent's Bread, Knowledge and Freedom (1981) had already demonstrated the important role of reading in inspiring working-class consciousness in early nineteenth-century Britain. As a sociologist, Long concluded that the really important question that needed answering was why academics did not care about readers.

passage: Christopher Columbus of Spain set foot in the New World in 1492. Six years later, Vasco da Gama of Portugal reached India. During the next two centuries the Spaniards and the Portuguese actively transferred, not only to Europe but to many parts of Asia as well, a number of plant species which they encountered in South and central America, in expectation of their potential either as food or as medicine. These plants had been developed to a high degree by the Maya and Inca civilizations of these regions. Of these, the potato (Solanum tuberosum) is believed to have been domesticated in terraced slopes on the high plateau of Bolivia-Peru in South America, sometime between 5000 and 2000 BC. Europeans first saw potatoes in South America in 1537, and around 1570 a Spanish ship brought the first potatoes to Europe. Though termed papa in South America, they were incorrectly called batata (the name for the sweet potato) when John Gerard first described them in English in 1597, and this name stuck. An 1860 report states that by 1780, potatoes, peas and beans were in high repute as foods in Calcutta, and that the Dutch are said to have been the first to introduce the culture of potatoes, which was received from their settlement of the Cape of Good Hope.
